title: Task Record Contract
description: Machine-checkable form of one task in the CROSS-HARNESS TASK STORE (Phase 0.2 — docs/STATE_LAYER.md's deferred 'Tasks CLI', ported from Hermes' kanban design per kb/wiki/synthesis/2026-07-19-hermes-codebase-fork-study.md: durable board, claim-leases (host:pid:uuid), heartbeats, claimed/completed/crashed/reclaimed lifecycle). A SIBLING of mission.schema.json — that schema tracks a MISSION's five dependency gates; this one tracks the much more granular 'task list, updates, accountability... whoever picked up a task and progress, cleared or stuck, resumable by any agent' unit Xavier's re-aimed vision calls for. File-per-task JSON at .tess/state/tasks/<id>.json (fenced instance data — see tess.manifest.json never_touch + this same file's own docs/STATE_LAYER.md). Every mutation goes through `tessctl tasks set|claim|release`, which dogfood-validate whatever they just wrote against THIS schema before returning (mirrors mission.schema.json's `_self_validate_or_raise` discipline) — an on-disk task record that fails its own schema is an internal engine bug, never a caller-visible outcome.

id.description: `T-<YYYYMMDD>-<kebab-slug>-<4hex>` — `tessctl tasks new <title>` derives this: an 8-digit UTC date, a truncated kebab-slug of the title (a human-readable hint, not the uniqueness guarantee), and a random 4-hex suffix that IS the uniqueness guarantee (so two tasks created the same day with the same title-prefix never collide, unlike mission.schema.json's id, which relies on a numeric collision suffix instead).

title.description: Human-readable task title, as given to `tessctl tasks new`.

status.description: The kanban column this task is currently in. `tessctl tasks new` seeds `backlog` by default; `tessctl tasks claim` auto-advances `backlog`/`ready` to `in_progress`; every other transition is an explicit `tessctl tasks set --status`.

owner.description: Human/team accountable for this task (distinct from `assignee`, the agent/persona currently doing the work, and from `claim`, the live claim-lease). null when not yet assigned.

assignee.description: Agent/persona currently assigned to this task (may be set before an actual claim-lease exists, e.g. during planning). null when not yet assigned.

target_harness.description: The routing LANE this task is earmarked for (Phase 0.4, issue #125 — the external-harness-worker lane): which harness SHOULD pick this task up, distinct from `created_by.harness` (who created it) and `claim`/the ledger `claim` event's `actor.harness` (who actually claimed it) — three separate facts this schema deliberately keeps separate rather than overloading one field for. Set via `tessctl tasks new|set --lane` (or implicitly by `tessctl tasks handoff --harness`); read via `tessctl tasks pull --lane`, which matches a task earmarked for the requested lane OR earmarked `any`. `any` — the default `tessctl tasks new` seeds when `--lane` is omitted — means eligible for every harness, i.e. the exact pre-lane behavior: a task nobody explicitly earmarks is filtered and claimed identically to before this field existed. This is advisory routing, not enforcement — the same trust-boundary class `claim` already documents in docs/STATE_LAYER.md — `tessctl tasks claim` does not refuse a claim whose `--harness` differs from a task's `target_harness`.

claim.description: The live claim-lease — who currently holds this task, cross-harness-resumable. All five fields are null together (unclaimed) or all five are set together (claimed); `_lint_task` flags a partially-set claim as a violation `tessctl validate` catches even though plain JSON Schema cannot express the all-or-nothing cross-field rule (same class of relational check `_lint_mission`/`_lint_crew_plan` already perform for their own schemas).

created_by.description: Which harness (and, optionally, which session of it) ran `tessctl tasks new` — the cross-harness provenance fact this whole subsystem exists to make durable (docs/STATE_LAYER.md: 'Tess OS is meant to run identically well from Claude Code, Codex, or any other AGENTS.md-reading harness... for state, not just doctrine').

created_at.description: UTC ISO-8601 timestamp ('...Z' suffix), set once at `tessctl tasks new` time.

updated_at.description: UTC ISO-8601 timestamp of the most recent successful `tasks set|claim|release` mutation. Bumped on EVERY write alongside `rev`.

rev.description: Optimistic-concurrency counter, starting at 1 and incremented by exactly 1 on every successful write. `tessctl tasks set --expected-rev N` is the CAS precondition: the write is refused (TASK_CAS_CONFLICT, no mutation) if the on-disk `rev` is not exactly N at write time — the caller must reload the current record and retry, the same ETag-style optimistic-concurrency-control pattern HTTP conditional requests use.

depends_on.description: Task ids this task depends on. `_lint_task` flags a task that lists itself, and duplicate entries — both relational checks plain JSON Schema cannot express.

evidence.description: Repo-relative paths (or other locators) backing this task's progress — the same 'a claim must be evidenced' spirit mission.schema.json's Gate.evidence already applies at the gate level, applied here per-task. APPEND-ONLY by convention: `tessctl tasks set --add-evidence` only ever appends; no CLI verb removes an entry (an accountability trail that could be silently pruned would defeat its own purpose).

notes.description: Free-text progress notes, APPEND-ONLY (same discipline as `evidence` — `tessctl tasks set --add-note` only ever appends).

blocked.description: The STRUCTURED STUCK-PACKET (Phase 0.5, issue #129) — null unless this task was blocked via `tessctl tasks block`. Distinct from the pre-existing `status: "blocked"` enum value: a task can still reach `blocked` status via a bare `tessctl tasks set --status blocked` (unchanged, pre-#129 behavior — this field stays null in that case), but `tasks block` additionally captures the resumable-by-any-agent context the bare status transition alone cannot: WHY it stopped, what state it was in, what was already tried, and what unblocks it. `tasks handoff`'s sibling: `handoff` = 'here's a task, go do it'; a `blocked` packet = 'I got stuck, here's everything you need to continue.' Set (a fresh packet, `blocked_at` always the CURRENT call's timestamp — a re-block is a genuine new event, not a heartbeat) by `tessctl tasks block <id>`; cleared to null as a side effect of `tessctl tasks set --status <anything other than blocked>` while the CURRENT status is `blocked` and a packet is present — an explicit accompanying decision, the same 'never silently un-block' discipline `claim` already applies to `status` itself, just applied here to the packet.

uuid.description: Claimant's own instance uuid (distinguishes two concurrent processes on the SAME host:pid across process-id reuse, and distinguishes two different sessions of the same harness).

claimed_at.description: UTC ISO-8601 timestamp of the ORIGINAL claim — unchanged across heartbeat refreshes by the same claimant.

heartbeat_at.description: UTC ISO-8601 timestamp of the most recent heartbeat (either an explicit `tessctl tasks set --heartbeat`, or an idempotent re-claim by the same host:pid:uuid). A future orphan-sweeper (NOT built by this region — see docs/STATE_LAYER.md) would compare this against a staleness threshold to decide a claim is abandoned; `tessctl tasks claim`'s own `--stale-after` does exactly that comparison today for the one caller-invoked case (another agent trying to claim the same task).

session.description: That harness's session id, if the caller supplied one.

at.description: UTC ISO-8601 timestamp the note was appended.

by.description: Who/what appended the note (defaults to the OS user if `--by` is omitted).

text.description: The note body. Never empty — an empty note carries no accountability information.

reason.description: WHY this task stopped, classified so a resuming agent (or a `tasks pull --status blocked` sweep, human or otherwise) can triage without reading free text first: `required_input` (missing credential/config/decision input), `failed_dependency` (an upstream task/system this one needs is not ready or errored), `gate` (a doctrine/review/CI gate refused to clear), `decision_needed` (a human/founder call is required — the guardrails.md Rule 18 hard-floor class), `other` (doesn't fit the above — `summary` carries the real reason).

summary.description: One-line human-readable statement of what blocked it — the first thing a resuming agent reads, same spirit as a ledger event's own `summary`.

progress.description: Last-known progress/state — what was accomplished before this task stopped, and exactly where it stopped, so a resuming agent does not have to reverse-engineer that from `evidence`/`notes` alone.

attempted.description: What was already tried (and did not resolve the block) — so a resuming agent does not repeat a dead end. May be empty (nothing was attempted yet before the block was recorded).

needed.description: What is needed to unblock — a credential, a decision, an upstream fix, a re-run once a dependency clears, etc. The single most actionable field in the packet.

blocked_at.description: UTC ISO-8601 timestamp this packet was recorded — set fresh on every `tessctl tasks block` call (a re-block, e.g. after a failed unblock attempt, is a genuinely NEW event, not a heartbeat refresh of the same one).

blocked_by.description: Which harness (and, optionally, which session of it) ran `tessctl tasks block` — reuses the SAME shape `created_by` already uses for the identical 'which harness, which session' provenance fact, applied here to who flagged the block instead of who created the task.

$comment: Minimal-validator keyword subset supported by tessctl validate: type, enum, const, properties, required, additionalProperties, items, minItems, maxItems, minLength, maxLength, pattern, minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, if/then/else, oneOf, anyOf, allOf, contains, $ref, $defs.
